text:
**The Case for Keeping Joined-Up Handwriting in Primary Schools**

Every few years, a new argument arrives that handwriting is obsolete. Children, we are told, will type for the rest of their lives, so the hours spent teaching them to link letters in looping chains are a nostalgic indulgence. Some schools have already acted on this, dropping cursive from the timetable or demoting it to an optional extra. I think this is a mistake. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting, and teach it properly, because it serves children's thinking, their fluency, their access to the written world, and their sense of themselves as writers. The case does not rest on tradition. It rests on what the skill does for the child holding the pen.

**What the evidence suggests about handwriting and thinking**

Begin with the strongest ground: handwriting is not merely a way of recording thought. It shapes thought. Research on early literacy has repeatedly found that children who learn letters by forming them by hand recognise and remember them better than children who learn them by typing or tracing on a screen. Studies using brain imaging, including work by Karin James and colleagues, have found that writing a letter by hand activates reading-related regions of the brain in a way that pressing a key does not. The movement itself, with its varied, effortful, self-generated strokes, appears to lay down a richer memory of what a letter is.

Joined-up writing extends this logic. When a child writes in a continuous flow, the hand must plan sequences rather than isolated marks. Each letter is shaped partly by the one before it and the one after. This is a more demanding motor task than printing, and it is exactly the sort of demanding task that builds fine motor control and the coordination between eye, hand and memory. Printed letters, produced one at a time with a lift of the pen between each, ask the child to start from scratch dozens of times per sentence. A joined hand turns the word into a single movement, which is closer to how we actually think of words: as wholes, not as piles of parts.

There is also a link to spelling. Because a cursive word is written as a unit, the child rehearses the sequence of letters in the word as a pattern. Teachers often report that children who struggle with spelling reversals and letter order find them easier when they learn to write words in a single flowing movement. The evidence here is less conclusive than for letter recognition, and honesty requires saying so, but the direction of the findings is consistent, and the mechanism is plausible. A word written in one motion is rehearsed as one thing.

**Fluency and the problem of working memory**

The second argument concerns speed and cognitive load. A young writer has limited working memory. Every ounce of attention spent on forming letters is attention not spent on composing sentences, choosing words, or remembering what the story needs next. Research by Steve Graham and others has shown that handwriting fluency predicts the quality and length of children's written composition, even after controlling for other factors. Children who write slowly and laboriously tend to write less, and to write worse, because the mechanics crowd out the thinking.

Here joined-up handwriting earns its place. Once learned, a fluent joined hand is faster than print. It avoids the constant pen lifts and restarts that slow printing down. A child who has automated a joined script can get their ideas onto the page at something closer to the speed they occur. Automaticity is the goal, and it only arrives through practice, which is why handwriting needs explicit, regular teaching rather than being left to chance.

The sceptic will reply that typing offers the same fluency, and in the long run that is true. But typing fluency is itself a skill that must be taught, and it cannot be acquired properly until children have the hand size, finger strength, and reading ability to do it. Seven-year-olds typing with two fingers are no faster than seven-year-olds writing by hand, and they lose the benefits described above. Teaching handwriting well in the early years and keyboard skills later is not a contradiction. It is sensible sequencing.

**Access to the written world**

A third argument is more practical and often overlooked. Cursive is how a great deal of the world is written. Birthday cards, handwritten notes from grandparents, recipes, letters, historical documents, signatures, and the marginal comments teachers leave on work are all written in joined script. A child who cannot read cursive is cut off from all of it. A child who cannot write it cannot produce a signature that looks like their own, or take quick notes in the flowing hand most adults use.

This is not a trivial concern. In the United States, where cursive was removed from the Common Core curriculum in 2010, teachers and archivists began reporting that young people could not read the Declaration of Independence in its original form or a letter from a great-grandparent. Several states have since moved to restore cursive instruction. The lesson is that skills dropped as unnecessary have a way of becoming necessary again, and that reading a script is much easier to learn when you have also written it.

There is also a question of equity. Children from homes full of books, devices, and adults who write by hand pick up a lot informally. Children from less advantaged homes depend more on school to teach them what others absorb at the kitchen table. If schools stop teaching joined-up writing, the gap between those who learn it anyway and those who do not will widen, and the second group will include children who are already behind. A good school curriculum is, among other things, a promise that everyone gets taught the things that matter, not just those whose parents happen to know to teach them.

**Handwriting, identity and dignity**

The fourth argument is the hardest to measure and perhaps the most human. A child's handwriting is theirs. It is recognisable, personal, and improves visibly over time. Many children take real pride in a neat joined hand, and the pen licence or the moment a teacher allows pen instead of pencil is a small rite of passage in countless classrooms. This is not sentimental. Motivation matters in school, and visible, achievable progress in a skill is motivating, especially for children who find other subjects difficult.

For children with certain learning differences the picture is mixed and deserves care. Some children with dyslexia report that cursive helps them, because the continuous movement reduces letter reversals and makes word boundaries clearer. Others with motor difficulties find any handwriting hard and benefit from alternatives such as keyboards. The right answer is not to abolish the skill but to teach it well to everyone and to provide alternatives where a child genuinely needs them. Removing cursive for all because some children struggle is like abolishing swimming lessons because some children are afraid of water.

**Answering the objections**

The most common objection is time. The curriculum is crowded, the argument goes, and every minute spent on cursive is a minute not spent on mathematics, science, or coding. But handwriting does not need hours. Short, frequent, well-structured practice, ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week, is far more effective than long sessions, and it can be folded into spelling and composition rather than treated as a separate subject. The cost is small. The benefits, as outlined above, reach into reading, spelling, composition and motor development.

A second objection is that employers and universities do not care about handwriting. This is partly true, and no one is arguing that children should be graded on penmanship in adulthood. But the argument for teaching a skill in primary school is not that every adult will use it daily. We teach children to swim, to draw, to play a recorder, and to do long division by hand, not because they will do these things constantly, but because the learning itself builds capacities that last. Joined-up handwriting belongs in this company.

A third objection is that the research is mixed, and some of it is. A fair reading says that the evidence for cursive over print specifically is weaker than the evidence for handwriting over typing in early years. Some studies find no advantage in speed or legibility for cursive. I accept this. The strongest claim I can make is not that cursive is magically superior, but that a fluent joined hand is a reasonable, efficient, widely used script, that it has demonstrated benefits for many children, and that there is no compelling evidence that dropping it improves outcomes. When a long-standing practice has plausible benefits and no demonstrated harm, the burden of proof lies with those who would abandon it.

**What good teaching looks like**

If primary schools keep joined-up handwriting, they should do it well. That means starting with pre-cursive foundations in the early years, such as pattern-making, correct pencil grip, and posture. It means introducing joins gradually once letter formation is secure, rather than rushing. It means choosing a single consistent style across the school so that children are not confused by changing models. And it means making space for practice that is short, regular, and tied to real writing, not drill for its own sake.

It also means being honest with children about purpose. Handwriting is not taught so that every note a child writes will be beautiful. It is taught so that writing becomes easy enough to be forgotten, freeing the mind to attend to what is being said. When the hand knows what to do, the child can think.

**Conclusion**

The case against teaching joined-up handwriting is superficially modern but substantively thin. It assumes that because a tool is new, the older skill has no remaining value, and it ignores what we know about how children learn. Handwriting builds letter knowledge, supports spelling, frees working memory for composition, opens access to a world written in script, and gives children a personal, achievable skill to be proud of. It costs little time when taught well. It can coexist with keyboard instruction rather than compete with it.

Primary schools should keep teaching it, and teach it with confidence. A child who can write fluently by hand has one more way to think, one more way to be understood, and one more door open. In an age that offers so many ways to avoid the effort of making marks, the effort itself is part of what we are teaching.
